title: QUIC vs HTTP/2 for LLM streaming through edge proxies - exploratory probe
content:
Summary:

This is a working note for an exploratory benchmark comparing QUIC (HTTP/3) vs HTTP/2 for streaming token-delivery during LLM inference across typical Redwood edge proxy chains. The focus is the incremental networking and transport overhead to the serving runtime in realistic topologies: single edge, edge + regional proxy, and a two-proxy chain. This doc records methodology, raw observations, and immediate recommendations. Still rough — TODO: re-run with larger sample size and more models.

Motivation / context:
- Many of our serving customers are latency-sensitive (chat/assistants). Network stacks and proxy chains amplify tail latency.
- We have ongoing work to support QUIC at the edge proxy (RFC-based stack) and need empirical guidance on whether enabling QUIC yields measurable benefits for streaming inference vs sticking with gRPC/HTTP2.
- Existing experiments look at chunking and proxy buffering; this probe focuses on transport-level effects (multiplex head-of-line, retransmit patterns, TLS handshake/resumption, and connection churn impact).

High-level takeaway (rough):
- QUIC reduced p95 incremental transport overhead by ~30-50% in chained-proxy topologies compared to HTTP/2 in our tests. Median improvements were smaller (~10–20%).
- When connection churn is high (short lived client connections per request), QUIC with 0-RTT resumption and connection migration shows the largest wins.
- For single-proxy, well-kept HTTP/2 connections with proper keepalive have similar medians to QUIC; differences show up under loss, reorder, and extra proxy hops.

Experiment design (quick notes):
- Workload: synthetic streaming inference using a small local LLM shard (redwood-test/llm-mini) producing tokenized chunks. Each client request asks for a 256-token stream emitted in 16-token chunks with 50ms server-side think-delay mimic. This isolates per-chunk networking overhead from model compute.
- Topologies tested: direct (no proxy), 1-edge-proxy (single Envoy-like terminator), 2-proxy chain (edge -> regional -> origin). Proxies are configured with default buffering and default http1/2 upgrades; QUIC tests used a Quiche-based proxy build.
- Client population: 100 concurrent clients, ramped for 10 minutes. Measured 5 runs per configuration.
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99 of per-chunk first-byte latency (time between client send and first token chunk arrival), connection setup latency, rebuffer events, number of packets retransmitted (simulated 0.1% packet loss for some runs).
- Instrumentation: client-side trace id propagated; we capture transport layer timestamps in proxy logs, and server token emit timestamps. Tools: wrk2-like generator for HTTP/2, quicly for HTTP/3; tcpdump on proxies for retransmit analysis.

Configs (representative):
- HTTP/2: h2 over TLS 1.3, keepalive ping: 30s, max concurrent streams: 100.
- QUIC: TLS 1.3 over QUIC (draft-29 stack), 0-RTT enabled, connection migration toggled off for baseline.
- Packet loss: 0% baseline, 0.1% and 0.5% for stress runs (emulated with tc-netem on proxy interfaces).

Representative raw numbers (median of 5 runs, per-chunk first-byte incremental overhead above local loop baseline where server compute -> 0ms):
- Direct (no proxy): HTTP/2 median=3.8ms, p95=14ms; QUIC median=3.5ms, p95=13ms
- 1-edge-proxy: HTTP/2 median=7.2ms, p95=34ms; QUIC median=5.9ms, p95=23ms
- 2-proxy chain: HTTP/2 median=11.6ms, p95=78ms, p99=220ms; QUIC median=8.4ms, p95=45ms, p99=120ms
- 2-proxy + 0.1% loss: HTTP/2 p95 jump to ~140ms, QUIC p95 to ~60ms

Notes on numbers / interpretation:
- HTTP/2 suffers from head-of-line blocking effects at the TCP layer when multiple chunk frames are sent and retransmits occur across proxy hops. Multiplexing benefits are real but break down with loss across multiple TCP legs.
- QUIC's per-stream independence and its recovery semantics reduced large tail events. We observed fewer long retransmit-induced stalls.
- Connection churn test (clients creating a new connection per request, median request interarrival 1s): HTTP/2 connections incurred ~110–185ms extra cost due to TLS handshakes and slow start when not reusing connections; with HTTP/2 keepalive and pooled connections this is mitigated but increases server resource usage. QUIC with 0-RTT kept initial request latency ~20–30ms lower in churn scenario.

Server/proxy observations:
- Edge proxy CPU: QUIC increased CPU usage by ~10–15% for the proxy binary in baseline encryption handling compared to HTTP/2 TLS offload path in our optimized binary. But tail latency win tended to outweigh CPU cost in latency-sensitive paths.
- Memory: QUIC per-connection state larger (quic control blocks), but manageable at expected connection counts.
- Socket-level: we saw a drop in RTT variance when QUIC was used for multi-hop paths because packet losses recovered locally without cross-TCP retransmit coupling.

Instrumentation snippets and commands used (for reproducibility):
- HTTP/2 client harness (wrk2-based): 
  ./wrk2 -t12 -c100 -d600s --h2 -R 500 --script=streaming.lua https://edge-host/infer
- QUIC client harness (quicly-based): 
  ./quic-gen --concurrency 100 --session-resumption --streaming --url https://edge-host/infer --script streaming-quic.lua
- Netem to apply loss on proxy egress: sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem loss 0.1% delay 1ms
- tcpdump capture filter: tcpdump -w run.pcap -i any host 10.0.3.5

Open issues / TODOs (short checklist):
- Re-run across a broader set of models (13B/70B quantized) to ensure results generalize when server-side token inter-arrival varies.
- Test QUIC with connection migration enabled to see mobile-client scenarios.
- Evaluate CPU/cost tradeoffs at production scale (brokered measurements across 4-node proxy clusters).
- Confirm findings with different proxy implementations (Envoy quic-summit vs our Quiche fork).
- Add real-user-like bursty think-times and longer tail tokens (512–2048 tokens) to stress streaming ordering.

Immediate recommendations (draft):
- Roll out QUIC as an opt-in on edge proxies for latency-sensitive routes (chat endpoints) in the next experiment stage. Track p95/p99 tail and proxy CPU delta.
- For short-lived connections (serverless clients or mobile clients creating new connections per request) enable 0-RTT and favor QUIC where available.
- Keep HTTP/2 as a supported fallback: for well-managed persistent connections HTTP/2 remains reasonable and more CPU-efficient at our current proxy build.

Quick notes to self / unresolved thoughts:
- Did not fully instrument client-side retransmit visibility for QUIC; need a finer-grained pcap + qlog correlation.
- Where we see large p99 reductions, is it because of queueing discipline differences in the proxy binary rather than transport? Need to control for proxy config more strictly.

If you want this converted to a slide-friendly short brief I can extract the key graphs and put into a 3-slide deck. Next run: add 0.5% loss and test with model-emitted jitter (random 0–30ms between tokens) and rerun 10x for stability.

---
Notes: this is a working doc; numbers are from early probes and intended to guide whether to invest in QUIC at the edge for streaming inference. Ping me if you want raw pcap/qlog artifacts.
